PREEN: Exemplar-Based Color Style Transfer with Smartphone Editor Presets
(Supplementary Material)

Beomjin Ahn
Samsung Research
Seoul, Korea
beomjin.ahn@samsung.com    Beomjin Ahn
Samsung Research
Seoul, Korea
beomjin.ahn@samsung.com
Abstract

We present PREEN (Preset Regression via an Exemplar-based Editor Network), which casts color style transfer as regression onto the 2929 parameters of a deterministic image editor. Given a content image and a style reference, PREEN predicts a preset, a vector of editor slider values that is interpretable and editor-consumable, not a raster image. The key obstacle is supervision, since an arbitrary real reference lacks a preset ground truth. We therefore supervise with a style-transfer teacher, whose target looks we invert into the editor’s parameter space as pseudo-presets, then pretrain a CLIP-conditioned regressor and refine it with LoRA under an image-level CIELAB loss. On the human-curated PST50 benchmark, PREEN applies the reference’s color while preserving structural fidelity, leading the baselines on pixel- and perceptual-fidelity metrics. The preset is compact and predicted at sub-second on-device latency. The low-dimensional subspace also exposes a single inference-time strength knob that traces a continuous default-to-vivid trajectory in one forward pass, with every intermediate state a valid editor preset. A two-axis human study shows that raters prefer the vivid end for matching the reference but the default as a standalone photo, a trade-off the knob spans without retraining.

1 Introduction

Exemplar-based color style transfer, also studied as photorealistic style transfer (PST), is a routine operation in modern photo editing. A user picks a reference image YY whose look they admire, wanting their own shot XX recolored to match it (Figure 1). Mainstream academic approaches are pixel-generative, from neural style transfer [13] to diffusion editing [23]. Whatever their quality, they emit rasters with no exposed editing parameters, and the diffusion-based ones add multi-second latency and stochastic sampling that resists deterministic re-editing, an awkward fit for on-device, user-in-the-loop consumer pipelines.

An alternative is photo preset transfer [6], predicting the parameters PP of a deterministic image editor EE from the pair (X,Y)(X,Y) such that E⁡(X,P)E(X,P) approximates the look of YY. The output PP, a vector of slider values, is interpretable and compact. Unlike a rendered image, it can be stored and re-edited, with no generative model at inference time.

The central challenge is supervision. Parametric retouching benchmarks such as MIT-Adobe FiveK [2] and PPR10K [19] provide human-authored target edits, but operate in the auto-enhancement regime without a separate style reference. No large-scale dataset pairs a content image with a reference and a matching expert-graded target. The principal prior method [6] sidesteps this by sampling presets, thereby bounding the styles it learns; the only reference-conditioned set with expert-graded targets we know of [4] offers just 50 pairs (PST50) for evaluation.

We close this gap with teacher supervision. We propose PREEN (Preset Regression via an Exemplar-based Editor Network). At inference, it maps a content–reference pair (X,Y)(X,Y) to a 2929-parameter preset that a smartphone editor applies to produce the result (Figure 2). A two-stage pipeline trains it. Phase 1 pretrains a CLIP-conditioned regressor on a large corpus of pseudo-labeled triples recovered from a style-transfer teacher. Phase 2 freezes all base weights and trains only low-rank adapters under an image-level CIELAB loss evaluated on the differentiable editor output, addressing the perceptual non-uniformity of Phase 1’s parameter-space loss.

Our contributions are: (i) a teacher-supervised recipe that frees reference-based preset regression from sampled-preset supervision, substituting a style-transfer teacher on real references; (ii) a strength-interpolation primitive, an inference-time scalar α\alpha on the chromaticity parameters that traces a continuous default-to-vivid trajectory without re-running inference; and (iii) a two-axis human study surfacing a three-way fidelity / style-match / aesthetic divergence across the α\alpha trajectory.

2 Related Work

2.1 Photo Preset Transfer

Editing photos by predicting the parameters of interpretable white-box operations has a long history. Learning-based automatic retouching predicts sequences of editing operations [12], and the same idea recurs in compositing harmonization [15]. Both regress parameters toward a fixed goal, enhancement or in-image harmonization, rather than a separate style reference. Deep Preset [6] established the reference-conditioned setting we adopt, regressing an editor preset (69 develop controls) from a content–reference pair, but its supervision is synthetic by construction. Training references are images re-rendered with sampled presets, so a ground-truth preset always exists, but the styles it can learn are confined to that sampled set. The setting has remained underexplored since then; the closest later work, NCST [14], regresses a smaller global-only parameter set from a reference to perform video grading. We revisit it without sampled-preset supervision: a style-transfer teacher on real reference pairs supplies targets we invert into the editor’s parameter space as pseudo-presets (Section 3).

2.2 Look-Up-Table Stylization

A separate line maps colors through a learned look-up table (LUT), a discretized grid over the RGB cube. Image-adaptive 3D LUT [35] and NLUT [3] predict one such grid applied uniformly across the image, and AceTone [22] predicts one from a reference with a vision-language model. Spatially aware variants blend multiple LUTs per pixel [33], and SA-LUT [4] extends these to a spatially adaptive 4D LUT, which we adopt as our teacher. SA-LUT also contributes the human-curated PST50 benchmark used for our evaluation (Section 4.2). Either way, the output is a dense grid of 10410^{4}–10510^{5} values (Table 1) rather than a few named sliders, leaving the edit hard for a user to inspect or refine.

2.3 Pixel-Generative Stylization

A large body of work renders stylization through pixel transformations, from classic global color-statistic transfer [11] to AdaIN [13], diffusion-based editing such as SDEdit [23], and recent neural color-style methods including Neural Preset [7], ModFlows [18], and INRetouch [5]. Concurrent work pushes further into generative modeling. SemiNFT [34] casts reference preset transfer as a Diffusion-Transformer task refined with reinforcement learning for aesthetic perception. These methods emit a raster image directly, without exposing user-editable parameters.

Neither the LUT nor the pixel-generative family yields an editable preset; we compare experimentally against both families and against Deep Preset, which targets the same task.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

Let E:𝒳×𝒫→𝒳E:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{X} denote a deterministic image editor mapping a content image XX and a parameter vector P∈[−1,1]dP\in[-1,1]^{d} to an edited image E⁡(X,P)E(X,P). We target a d=29d=29 editor representative of consumer mobile photo applications: 88 global controls (temperature, tint, brightness, exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, saturation) and 2121 per-hue HSL channels (hue/saturation/luminance for each of 77 color zones: red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue, magenta). We split the 2929 parameters into a tone set ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} (1212: contrast, brightness, exposure, highlights, shadows, per-hue luminance) and a chromaticity set ℐab\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ab}} (1717: temperature, tint, saturation, per-hue hue/saturation). Equivalently, the 88 global controls split 55 tone / 33 chroma and the 2121 per-hue channels split 77 / 1414, a split reused by the regressor’s two output trunks (Section 3.3) and the α\alpha control (Section 3.5). We implement these controls, inspired by consumer smartphone photo editors, as a differentiable module (stage-by-stage pipeline in the supplementary), so both the Phase 1 inversion (Eq. 1) and the Phase 2 image-level loss can backpropagate through EE, the same module that produces every PREEN result we report. Given (X,Y)(X,Y), the goal is a regressor fθ​(X,Y)=Ppredf_{\theta}(X,Y)=P_{\mathrm{pred}} such that Xpred′=E⁡(X,Ppred)X^{\prime}_{\mathrm{pred}}=E(X,P_{\mathrm{pred}}) approximates the look of YY.

3.2 Teacher Supervision

We instantiate the teacher with SA-LUT [4], a spatially adaptive 4D LUT producing a pseudo-target X~′=T⁡(X,Y)\tilde{X}^{\prime}=T(X,Y) for any pair. A LUT teacher is structure-preserving and dominated by color/tone transforms that lie close to our editor’s subspace, unlike a pixel-generative teacher’s edits. Both phases use the published teacher unmodified; a spatially global variant appears only in the ablation (Table 3).

3.3 Phase 1: Pseudo-Label Recovery and Regression

For each (X,X~′)(X,\tilde{X}^{\prime}), we project the teacher’s richer edit into the editor’s constrained 2929-parameter subspace, recovering a pseudo-preset P~\tilde{P} by gradient-based optimization through the differentiable editor [32]:

P~=arg⁡minP∈[−1,1]29​ℒrec​(E⁡(X,P),X~′),\tilde{P}=\arg\min_{P\in[-1,1]^{29}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}\!\bigl(E(X,P),\,\tilde{X}^{\prime}\bigr), (1)

where ℒrec=MSERGB+λlab​(MSEL∗+MSEa∗​b∗)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{RGB}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{lab}}\bigl(\mathrm{MSE}_{L^{*}}+\mathrm{MSE}_{a^{*}b^{*}}\bigr), each term the mean-squared error between E⁡(X,P)E(X,P) and X~′\tilde{X}^{\prime} over the indicated channels, an RGB anchor plus CIELAB luminance and chromaticity, and the weight λlab\lambda_{\mathrm{lab}} is set on a held-out subset. We run AdamW for a fixed step budget per pair, yielding the (X,Y,P~)(X,Y,\tilde{P}) triples on which the regressor below is trained.

The regressor fθf_{\theta} is a frozen CLIP visual encoder [10] feeding a simple residual MLP. Both XX and YY pass through the shared encoder, and we concatenate the per-image 768768-d CLIP image embeddings (the projected encoder output) with five handcrafted color-statistic features of XX and YY: (i) the RGB log-ratio log⁡(μY/μX)\log(\mu_{Y}/\mu_{X}), (ii) the HSL channel-mean difference, (iii) low-level RGB mean/std, (iv) a soft RGB color histogram, and (v) per-channel RGB percentile differences. These low-frequency color statistics supplement CLIP’s semantic features. The MLP runs two parallel residual trunks over this shared vector, each [1024,1024,1024,256][1024,1024,1024,256]: a tone trunk ending in a linear head for the ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} parameters and a chroma trunk for the ℐab\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ab}} parameters, each head applying Softsign so Ppred∈[−1,1]29P_{\mathrm{pred}}\in[-1,1]^{29}. Phase 1 minimizes ℒph1=H0.1​(Ppred−P~)+λ​‖Ppred‖22\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ph1}}=H_{0.1}\!\bigl(P_{\mathrm{pred}}-\tilde{P}\bigr)+\lambda\|P_{\mathrm{pred}}\|_{2}^{2} with the CLIP backbone frozen, where H0.1H_{0.1} is the Huber loss (β=0.1\beta\!=\!0.1) and the ℓ2\ell_{2} term lightly regularizes the predicted preset.

3.4 Phase 2: Adaptation under Image-Level Loss

Phase 1 already yields a working regressor, but its parameter-space loss is not perceptually uniform. Because a ±0.1\pm 0.1 shift in brightness is far more visible than the same shift in a per-hue blue-hue parameter, Phase 2 refines the model with an image-level loss, matching the edited image so that capacity concentrates on the perceptually salient changes that the parameter-space loss underweights.

Phase 2 freezes all base weights of fθf_{\theta} and trains only rank-16 LoRA adapters [11] on every CLIP attention and FFN projection. Adapters of the same rank are also placed on every linear layer of the MLP. After training, the adapters are merged, leaving inference cost identical to that of Phase 1. The Phase 2 objective passes predicted presets through the differentiable editor and applies a CIELAB reconstruction loss between Xpred′=E⁡(X,Ppred)X^{\prime}_{\mathrm{pred}}=E(X,P_{\mathrm{pred}}) and X~′\tilde{X}^{\prime}, plus an ℓ2\ell_{2} regularizer on PpredP_{\mathrm{pred}}:

ℒph2=wpix​ℒpix+wab​ℒab+wL​ℒL+λ​‖Ppred‖22,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ph2}}=w_{\mathrm{pix}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pix}}+w_{\mathrm{ab}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ab}}+w_{L}\mathcal{L}_{L}+\lambda\|P_{\mathrm{pred}}\|_{2}^{2}, (2)

where ℒab\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ab}}, ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L}, and the auxiliary anchor ℒpix\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pix}} are mean-squared errors in CIELAB a∗​b∗a^{*}b^{*}, L∗L^{*}, and RGB, with (wpix,wab,wL)=(0.2,5.0,1.0)(w_{\mathrm{pix}},w_{\mathrm{ab}},w_{L})=(0.2,5.0,1.0) set on a held-out subset. The term ℒL\mathcal{L}_{L} backpropagates only into the tone trunk and ℒab\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ab}} only into the chroma trunk (the complementary slice is detached). The RGB anchor reaches both. The ℓ2\ell_{2} regularizer reuses the Phase 1 weight λ\lambda and keeps parameters at 00 when they have little effect (e.g., HSL channels with no corresponding color present).

The Phase 2 target is the full teacher applied to an augmented reference YaugY_{\mathrm{aug}} (a random crop/flip of YY; Section 4.1), X~′=T⁡(X,Yaug)\tilde{X}^{\prime}=T(X,Y_{\mathrm{aug}}). Identity samples (Y=XY\!=\!X, at a 0.10.1 ratio) use XX itself as the target.

3.5 Strength Interpolation via ℐab\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ab}} α\alpha-Scaling

Operating in an explicit low-dimensional parameter subspace admits a parameter-space controllability primitive. At editing time, a scalar α\alpha rescales the chromaticity slice ℐab\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ab}} of PpredP_{\mathrm{pred}} (Section 3.1), leaving the tone set ℐL\mathcal{I}_{L} unchanged, to dial edit intensity. We define

Piα={α​Pi1+(α−1)​|Pi|,i∈ℐab,Pi,i∈ℐL.P^{\alpha}_{i}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\alpha\,P_{i}}{1+(\alpha-1)\,|P_{i}|},&i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ab}},\\[4.0pt] P_{i},&i\in\mathcal{I}_{L}.\end{cases} (3)

This form is simply the head’s Softsign (P=z/(1+|z|)P\!=\!z/(1{+}|z|)) re-applied after rescaling its pre-activation z↦α​zz\!\mapsto\!\alpha z, so α=1\alpha\!=\!1 recovers PpredP_{\mathrm{pred}} and it inherits Softsign’s sign- and [−1,1][-1,1]-preservation with smooth saturation as α→∞\alpha\!\to\!\infty. Setting α>1\alpha\!>\!1 thus intensifies the entire predicted color edit (saturation and hue shifts alike), producing a vivid, stronger variant that emphasizes color shift over fidelity to the teacher distribution.

Restricting the rescaling to chroma is deliberate, since rescaling luminance parameters as well co-saturates global tone, clips highlights, and crushes shadows (supplementary). Chroma-only scaling preserves the tonal anchor while the color identity intensifies, and one fθf_{\theta} serves both modes.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Content images XX are drawn from OpenImages [17], and style references YY from the top 20%20\% of the AVA aesthetics database [26] by mean aesthetic score, so references are well-composed, attractively graded photos. We embed every image with CLIP ViT-L/14 [10] and pair each XX with one of its top-1010 nearest references by cosine similarity, so the reference is semantically compatible, not arbitrary. This yields a few hundred thousand (X,Y)(X,Y) training pairs, supervised by the SA-LUT [4] teacher. The Phase 1 pseudo-presets P~\tilde{P} are recovered via Eq. 1.

All optimizers are AdamW [20]. Phase 1 inversion (Eq. 1) runs 1,0001{,}000 steps at learning rate 0.20.2 per pair with the CIELAB weight λlab=20\lambda_{\mathrm{lab}}\!=\!20, chosen on a held-out subset, and a small pre-activation magnitude decay (10−310^{-3}). Phase 1 regression uses learning rate 3×10−53{\times}10^{-5}. Phase 2 trains rank-16 LoRA at learning rate 1×10−41{\times}10^{-4}, batch size 6464, bf16, λ=10−2\lambda=10^{-2}, on an NVIDIA L4 GPU. The augmentation YaugY_{\mathrm{aug}} is a random square crop (8080–100%100\% of the short side) plus a horizontal flip.

4.2 Evaluation

We evaluate on PST50 [4], a human-curated benchmark of (content, reference, expert-edited target) triples. We adopt the four metrics reported with it: PSNR, SSIM, HCorr (per-channel HSV histogram similarity to the target), and LPIPS [15], all computed on outputs and ground truth resized to 256×256256{\times}256, SA-LUT’s training resolution. We additionally report Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab}, the mean CIELAB color difference to the expert target, used as an evaluation metric in the paired-target retouching literature [19, 35], where CIELAB-space training losses are also common [24, 25].

4.3 Main Results on PST50

Table 1 reports the five PST50 metrics (Section 4.2) averaged over the paired triples. NCST [14], another parametric prior, is not benchmarked, as it releases no public code or weights and was not evaluated on PST50.

PREEN improves on Deep Preset in both its forms, the generator’s rendered output Y^\hat{Y} (a raster) and the predicted preset P^\hat{P} applied in Lightroom. In Table 1, it leads every baseline on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, by +1.34+1.34 dB PSNR over Deep Preset (Y^\hat{Y}), +1.20+1.20 dB over the next-best NLUT, and +1.96+1.96 dB over the no-edit (identity) row, while lifting HCorr from 0.3480.348 (no-edit) to 0.4730.473, though it trails most free-form Raster/LUT baselines there. On Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} (9.079.07), it ties the LUT methods within per-image noise (supplementary). Section 5 discusses how the restrained PST50 targets shape these scores.

A global preset lacks the local adaptivity of spatially varying baselines such as SA-LUT. What Table 1 shows is that, on this benchmark, the 2929-parameter representation is not itself the bottleneck. It stays within range of LUT grids over 1000×1000\times larger in dimension (ℝ3×2×173\mathbb{R}^{3\times 2\times 17^{3}} vs. ℝ29\mathbb{R}^{29}; Table 1). The HCorr gap to the LUTs is prediction headroom, not a subspace limit (oracle HCorr 0.6720.672, supplementary). Figure 3 shows a head-to-head on the first five PST50 samples, where PREEN’s edit lands close to the expert target.

PREEN also generalizes beyond PST50. Figure 4 gives qualitative results on DPST [8] pairs (no paired ground truth, so no metrics). It restyles content on par with Deep Preset while retaining α\alpha control. The full PST50 grid, two more DPST pairs, the predicted presets for example pairs, and an in-the-wild gallery are in the supplementary.

4.4 Ablation Studies

4.4.1 Component Ablation

Table 2 isolates the contribution of each training phase. Phase 1 alone, a frozen-CLIP MLP regressor trained on pseudo-labels, already reaches 23.60 dB PSNR, above both Deep Preset forms. Phase 2 LoRA adaptation adds the largest gains, most prominently in chromaticity (→0.4730.383\!\to\!0.473 HCorr). By contrast, Phase 2 only, a single stage from random initialization with no Phase 1 that fully fine-tunes the MLP under the image-level loss and adapts CLIP via LoRA as in PREEN, does not surpass the full pipeline on the task’s target metrics. Although it edges SSIM, it trails on HCorr (0.4530.453 vs. 0.4730.473) and LPIPS and reaches only a comparable Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} (9.129.12 vs. 9.079.07) before peaking early and degrading, despite its larger fully fine-tuned capacity. The benefit of Phase 1’s initialization is thus not recovered by single-stage optimization; replacing that stage’s fine-tuning with LoRA fares worse still (Δ​Ea​b∗​ 9.57\Delta E^{*}_{ab}\,9.57; supplementary), consistent with a low-rank update on an untrained base being underexpressive and with Phase 1’s pretrained base enabling the efficient LoRA adaptation.

Single-factor variants locate the gains: MLP-only LoRA (frozen CLIP) keeps fidelity but recovers under half the chromaticity gain (HCorr 0.4230.423), so adaptation must reach the representation, not just the head; disabling the dual-trunk gradient routing (joint LL/a​bab gradients) costs 0.380.38 dB PSNR and 0.0160.016 SSIM at unchanged HCorr, confirming the routing aids tonal fidelity; and dropping identity samples collapses fidelity (SSIM 0.8330.833, PSNR below the no-edit floor). Removing the CIELAB terms (plain RGB MSE) instead gains pixel fidelity but cedes every color-facing metric (Table 2). A single RGB term underweights chroma, settling into damped color edits, whereas CIELAB lets us weight chroma above luminance (wab=5w_{\mathrm{ab}}\!=\!5 vs. wL=1w_{L}\!=\!1, Eq. 2), committing to the color transfer the task demands.

4.4.2 Teacher Choice

SA-LUT varies its edit across the image, whereas our editor applies one global preset, so Phase 1 must project spatially varying edits onto global parameters. To test whether a teacher matched to the editor yields cleaner pseudo-labels, we also tried a global variant that collapses SA-LUT’s per-pixel context map to a per-image mean. It brings no consistent improvement (Table 3). The variant edges PSNR by ∼0.1{\sim}0.1 dB and SSIM by 0.0030.003 but lowers HCorr (→0.4650.473\!\to\!0.465) and worsens Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} (→9.239.07\!\to\!9.23), the two metrics that score color most directly. The two teachers differ significantly on no metric (supplementary), so the published teacher can be used as is, without tailoring it to the editor.

4.4.3 Backbone Choice

We probe the backbone by swapping the frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder for three recent vision encoders at matched capacity and training budget (Table 4): the self-supervised DINOv3 [12], the contrastive SigLIP 2 [13], and the VLM-oriented InternViT [2, 3] (checkpoints in the supplementary). Removing the backbone entirely, leaving only the handcrafted color statistics, degrades every metric. The converse, CLIP without the handcrafted features, scores 23.1523.15 dB (not shown), between no-backbone (23.0323.03) and full (23.6023.60; Table 4), so the backbone and the color features contribute complementarily, neither subsuming the other. On PSNR, the backbones are close; on Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab}, only CLIP (10.6010.60) and InternViT beat the no-backbone floor (11.3611.36), with CLIP best. We adopt CLIP, the standard, widely deployed choice with mature on-device support.

4.4.4 Preset-Group Contribution

To see which of the 2929 parameters carry the edit, we mask the predicted preset during inference to retain only the specified groups, setting the rest to their neutral values (Table 5). The contribution is interpretable and largely monotonic. White balance alone (G1) sets the gross color cast (its PSNR sits below no-edit until tone joins), the global tone parameters (G2) add the largest single jump (+2.2+2.2 dB over G1), global saturation (G3) helps fidelity while dipping HCorr (→0.4430.451\!\to\!0.443), and the 2121 per-hue HSL channels (G4) close the remaining HCorr gap (→0.4730.443\!\to\!0.473), the color-fidelity component the global parameters cannot reach.

4.5 Strength Interpolation (α\alpha Sweep)

Figure 5 shows color saturation intensifying smoothly from α=1\alpha\!=\!1 through α=5\alpha\!=\!5 (Vivid) to α=10\alpha\!=\!10 with no re-inference. PSNR peaks at the default and degrades monotonically as α\alpha grows while perceptual saturation keeps increasing, a trade-off that motivates our two operating points. We fix Vivid at α=5\alpha\!=\!5 by visual inspection, not by tuning on the benchmark. The look is clearly intensified but not yet degenerate. The full per-α\alpha table and a luminance-rescale failure case are in the supplementary.

4.6 Off-the-Shelf Foundation Models

4.6.1 Direct Parameter Prediction

We prompt three frontier vision-language models (Gemini 3.1 Pro [5], Claude Opus 4.8 [1], and the open-weight Qwen3-VL 235B [9]) to predict the 2929 parameters from the content–reference pair, providing the full channel specification, valid ranges, and a forced structured-output schema, with one query per image (Table 6; verbatim prompt in the supplementary). Under a neutral prompt (ranges and sign conventions only), all three produce much larger edits and score worse on every metric of the supplementary comparison (PSNR −2.9-2.9 to −6.0-6.0 dB). The VLM rows of Table 6 therefore use the conservative guided prompt. They cluster at 21.421.4–22.522.5 dB PSNR, 2.12.1–3.23.2 dB below PREEN. Calibrating sliders from text alone, without the editor’s feedback, is hard.

4.6.2 Direct Pixel Synthesis

The complementary route skips parameters entirely. Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image) [8], run once per pair on PST50 and prompted to transfer the reference’s color and mood while preserving structure, matches PREEN on HCorr but trails it in fidelity by ∼5{\sim}5 dB PSNR, 0.170.17 SSIM, and over 2×2\times LPIPS (Table 6). Synthesized pixels drift from the content’s fine structure, and the output is a non-deterministic raster with no editable parameters.

4.7 User Study

Automatic metrics capture fidelity, not perceived quality. We run pairwise preference studies: PREEN Vivid (α=5\alpha\!=\!5) and the default each against (i) Deep Preset (P^\hat{P}) and (ii) Claude Opus 4.8 predicting the same preset, plus Vivid vs. default (isolating α\alpha) and both vs. the SA-LUT teacher. Raters judge style match (closer to the reference) and aesthetic appeal (more pleasing as a standalone photo). The VLM opponent uses its guided prompt (Section 4.6). Figure 6 reports PREEN’s win rates, and the supplementary lists each with its 95%95\% confidence interval.

On style match, Vivid wins against every compared preset opponent (Deep Preset 61.6%61.6\%, Claude 65.7%65.7\%, PREEN’s own default 73.4%73.4\%; pooled 66.9%66.9\%, [62.2,71.6][62.2,71.6]) and roughly ties the teacher itself (44.6%44.6\%, [36.2,53.3][36.2,53.3]), to which the default loses (28.3%28.3\%). On aesthetic appeal, the ordering inverts. Vivid drops to 43.3%43.3\% pooled, [38.9,47.9][38.9,47.9], with raters favoring the default and Claude as standalone images, yet both PREEN modes are preferred to the teacher’s full-strength edit (68.8%68.8\%/73.8%73.8\%).

This three-way split is the study’s central finding. The metrics rank the default highest, human style-match ranks Vivid highest, and standalone aesthetic preference returns to the default. “Matches the reference” and “looks best on its own” are different objectives. The α\alpha knob spans them without retraining.

The default also holds its own. It beats Deep Preset on both axes (61.8%61.8\% style, [53.0,70.6][53.0,70.6]; 67.5%67.5\% aesthetic, [60.6,74.0][60.6,74.0]) and roughly matches Claude Opus 4.8 (52.0%52.0\%/52.5%52.5\%) while remaining deterministic and far cheaper.

4.8 On-Device Deployment

We export fθf_{\theta} (LoRA merged) to TFLite with 8-bit dynamic-range quantization (INT8 weights, FP32 activations) and benchmark on a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 smartphone (8 CPU threads, median of 20 warm runs). The preset is predicted end-to-end in 283283 ms per pair, CPU-only. Latency is dominated by the CLIP backbone (304304M of 315315M parameters), yet within a sub-second UX budget. Quantization preserves accuracy. On PST50, the INT8 artifact scores 24.3424.34/0.9150.915/0.4790.479/0.0930.093/9.029.02, within 0.30.3 dB PSNR of Table 1 and matching it on the other four metrics.

5 Discussion and Limitations

More than the numbers, PREEN’s payoff is the form of its output, an interpretable, deterministic preset that an editor consumes directly. The explicit 2929-dimensional subspace also makes controllability free: a single inference-time scalar α\alpha rescales the preset’s chroma along a default-to-vivid trajectory of valid, re-editable presets. Across that trajectory, the three-way divergence that our user study surfaces (Figure 6) makes the best operating point a user preference, not a fixed target.

Beyond controllability, the fidelity numbers invite a second reading. A global preset is structurally more constrained than the spatial LUT teacher, so PREEN’s higher PST50 fidelity scores (Table 1) do not indicate greater expressivity; they reflect PST50’s restrained expert targets. The teacher overshoots these conservative edits, while PREEN’s identity sampling (Table 2) and ℓ2\ell_{2} preset regularizer keep it calibrated. Damping the teacher toward the input confirms this, improving it on four of the five PST50 metrics (full diagnostic in the supplementary).

PREEN also inherits the editor’s failure modes. Looks that remap color instead of adjusting it (split-toned monochromes, wholesale palette shifts) lie outside EE’s space, as do local effects such as grain, vignettes, and local burns; for the former, even the per-image oracle fails (supplementary). It also assumes a semantically compatible reference: our pairs are matched by content, and we do not test transfer to disjoint references. Shrinking the CLIP-dominated footprint (Section 4.8) with a lighter encoder (e.g., MobileCLIP or FastViT) is left to future work.

6 Conclusion

We presented PREEN, which recasts exemplar-based color style transfer as regression onto a deterministic editor’s 2929 parameters. Lacking ground-truth presets, we invert a style-transfer teacher’s output into the editor’s parameter space, train a CLIP-conditioned regressor, and adapt it with LoRA under an image-level CIELAB loss. On PST50, the preset recovers the reference’s color shift while preserving structure; it is interpretable, ∼1000×{\sim}1000\times more compact than the teacher’s LUT, and runs on-device in sub-second time. A single chromaticity scalar spans default and vivid looks, exposing strength as a free, re-editable control. A human study shows that the two ends of that range serve different goals, matching the reference and standing alone as a photo.

1 Editor Pipeline Details

The editor applies the 2929 parameters in a fixed order typical of consumer smartphone photo editors. Each parameter maps to a specific operator and stage (Table S1). Parameters act in [−1,1][-1,1] and are internally rescaled to the device ranges. Stages 1–4 operate in RGB, stages 5–8 on the BT.601 (Rec. 601) luma YY, and stage 9 in HSL with per-hue Gaussian masks. Every operation is differentiable almost everywhere, so gradients from the Phase 2 image-level loss flow back to PpredP_{\mathrm{pred}}.

Table S1 gives the update rule of every stage. The input pixel is X=(Xr,Xg,Xb)∈[0,1]3X=(X_{r},X_{g},X_{b})\in[0,1]^{3}, and we write s≡100​ps\equiv 100\,p for the (rescaled) parameter of each stage.

2 Full α\alpha Sweep Analysis

Table S3 reports the full chroma-only α\alpha sweep on PST50, extending the two operating points used in the main paper. Toward α→0\alpha\!\to\!0 the chroma edit is under-applied and the color-facing metrics (HCorr, Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab}) weaken, and for large α\alpha (55, 1010) over-saturation degrades every metric. Performance stays close to the α=1\alpha\!=\!1 values for small departures (α∈[0.5,2]\alpha\!\in\![0.5,2]) and falls off more clearly by α=3\alpha\!=\!3 (PSNR →23.5324.63\!\to\!23.53, Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} →10.299.07\!\to\!10.29). We adopt α=1\alpha\!=\!1 as the default operating point.

Why chroma-only? Luminance rescale co-saturates tone. Figure S1 contrasts our chroma-only α\alpha-scaling with rescaling all 2929 parameters (luminance included) on a PST50 sample with a pronounced warm edit. Chroma-only scaling intensifies the color identity while the tonal anchor stays fixed, so the image keeps a similar luminance scale even at α=10\alpha\!=\!10. Rescaling the luminance parameters also co-saturates exposure, brightness, and contrast, driving the tones toward crushed shadows or blown highlights and flattening the photograph as α\alpha grows. This motivates restricting the α\alpha knob to the chromaticity slice ℐab\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ab}}.

Does α\alpha rotate hue? A natural worry is that scaling the chromaticity parameters reorients hue rather than merely intensifying it. We bound the per-channel hue rotation the α\alpha knob actually applies (an upper bound, as the per-hue Gaussian weight wh≤1w_{h}\!\leq\!1), measured over the 77 per-hue channels of all 5050 PST50 images. At the default α=1\alpha\!=\!1 no per-hue channel rotates by more than 30∘30^{\circ} (median 2.1∘2.1^{\circ}), and even at the Vivid setting (α=5\alpha\!=\!5) only 0.3%0.3\% do (median 8.9∘8.9^{\circ}). Pushing to α=10\alpha\!=\!10, twice Vivid, still leaves the median at 14.9∘14.9^{\circ} with no channel beyond 60∘60^{\circ} and only 3.7%3.7\% past 30∘30^{\circ}. The editor’s bounded [−1,1][-1,1] per-hue range thus keeps hue identity largely intact as saturation grows.

3 Metric Protocol

Every method receives PST50’s Rec. 709 content, and outputs and the expert target are bilinearly resized to 256×256256{\times}256 (the SA-LUT [4] training resolution and kernel). PSNR is computed in sRGB. SSIM [14] uses an 11×1111{\times}11 Gaussian window (σ=1.5\sigma{=}1.5). HCorr is the mean per-channel correlation of 6464-bin HSV histograms. LPIPS [15] uses pyiqa’s lpips-vgg+, the VGG variant whose spatial average is weighted by semantic features. Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} is the mean per-pixel CIE76 difference ∥LAB⁡(X′)−LAB⁡(target)∥2\lVert\mathrm{LAB}(X^{\prime})-\mathrm{LAB}(\mathrm{target})\rVert_{2} in CIELAB. Times in Table 1 of the main paper are per-image latencies on an Intel Xeon 6975P-C CPU, with every method producing the same 256×256256{\times}256 output. The final checkpoint is chosen on a held-out validation split. PST50 is used only for the reported evaluation, and none of its images appear in our training data. We compute a perceptual hash (DCT pHash) for every training image and every PST50 image, and, for each PST50 image, rank every training image by pHash Hamming distance and inspect its closest matches. All are distinct photographs sharing at most coarse composition or tone, with no duplicates.

Baseline rendering. The Deep Preset (P^\hat{P}) [6] baseline predicts a Lightroom develop preset, which we apply to each content image and export in Adobe Lightroom Classic 15.2.1, one fixed build used for both the metrics in Table 1 of the main paper and the qualitative figures. Reinhard [11] is implemented as per-channel mean and standard-deviation transfer in CIELAB, and all other methods are rendered with their own released code. Neural Preset [7] is omitted because it releases neither model weights nor training code. It is also a neural color-mapping method rather than an editor-preset predictor.

4 Per-Image Statistical Tests

All methods are evaluated on the same 50 PST50 triples, so paired per-image tests apply. Table S4 reports PREEN’s mean per-image advantage on each metric (sign-preserving difference, PREEN minus baseline) with two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank pp-values. At the uncorrected 0.050.05 level, PREEN’s PSNR and SSIM advantages are significant against every baseline, and LPIPS against all but Deep Preset (Y^\hat{Y}) (p=.077p{=}.077). On Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab}, PREEN’s point-estimate lead over the two LUT methods (9.079.07 vs. 9.639.63/9.819.81) is within per-image noise (p≥.42p{\geq}.42), while all other Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} advantages are significant. The HCorr deficits to the free-form LUT/raster methods (negative entries) are prediction headroom rather than a subspace limit, since the oracle reaches HCorr 0.6720.672 (Table S5). In contrast, the HCorr gain over the no-edit baseline is significant (p<.001p{<}.001). Under per-metric Holm correction within the family of between-method comparisons (the eight upper-block rows), every PSNR advantage over a published method remains significant (adjusted p≤.031p{\leq}.031), while the marginal effects do not (SSIM vs. no edit/Deep Preset (P^\hat{P}); LPIPS vs. Deep Preset (Y^\hat{Y})/ModFlows; Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} vs. Deep Preset (Y^\hat{Y})/ModFlows). Finally, the last row is a separate within-method test. We detect no significant per-image difference between PREEN trained under the SA-LUT-global teacher variant and under the published teacher (all p≥.56p{\geq}.56), and the small color-metric gaps that do appear lean slightly toward the published teacher (the direction shown in Table 3 of the main paper). The global variant thus brings no consistent gain.

For absolute scale, PREEN’s own per-metric means carry 95%95\% bootstrap CIs (1010k resamples, n=50n{=}50): PSNR 24.63​[23.28,25.92]24.63\,[23.28,25.92], SSIM 0.914​[0.894,0.932]0.914\,[0.894,0.932], HCorr 0.473​[0.413,0.533]0.473\,[0.413,0.533], LPIPS 0.094​[0.081,0.107]0.094\,[0.081,0.107], and Δ​Ea​b∗​ 9.07​[7.83,10.41]\Delta E^{*}_{ab}\,9.07\,[7.83,10.41].

5 Training-Free Probes and Reference Points

We chart what training-free use of (X,Y)(X,Y) and the teacher affords, under the same protocol as Table 1 of the main paper. (i) Fit-to-reference optimizes, per pair, the 2929 editor parameters (AdamW, 1,2001{,}200 steps) so the edited content matches the reference’s color statistics, using either per-channel CIELAB mean and standard deviation, in the spirit of classic color transfer [11], or the full sorted CIELAB marginals, then applies the result at full resolution. (ii) Damped teacher output is the raster blend Xγ′=(1−γ)​X+γ​T​(X,Y)X^{\prime}_{\gamma}=(1{-}\gamma)X+\gamma\,T(X,Y) with the SA-LUT teacher, sweeping γ∈[0.1,1.0]\gamma\in[0.1,1.0] and reporting the best (γ=0.5\gamma{=}0.5). (iii) Test-time-optimization (TTO) inversion applies Eq. (1) of the main paper at test time to the teacher output (or to the damped teacher output), i.e., a preset-output method that needs the teacher plus a per-image optimization at inference (about one minute per image on the same CPU at 256×256256{\times}256, 1,0001{,}000 AdamW steps, vs. PREEN’s 0.360.36 s without the teacher). (iv) Oracle is the same inversion against the expert target, upper-bounding the editor’s subspace.

Table S5 reports the results, which carry four lessons.

First, reference-fitting reaches HCorr 0.4550.455/0.4710.471 under the two statistic-matching objectives (on par with PREEN’s 0.4730.473) yet collapses every fidelity metric below the no-edit baseline. The reference is a different scene, so its raw statistics are not the editing target, and over-applying them distorts the photograph (Figure S2, where PREEN’s restrained edits on the same samples stay close to the target). This is the characteristic failure of a distribution-only proxy and shows why HCorr must be read alongside fidelity.

Second, the damped teacher output shows how PST50’s restrained targets reward restraint. At γ=0.5\gamma{=}0.5, the blend surpasses most methods in Table 1 of the main paper. Calibrating other baselines’ edit strength does not close the gap: the same γ\gamma sweep lifts none of the other four learned raster/LUT baselines past PREEN’s 24.6324.63 dB (best blends: NLUT 24.0524.05, ModFlows 24.1624.16, Deep Preset (Y^\hat{Y}) 23.5223.52, AdaIN 23.5123.51 dB).

Third, projecting teachers into the editor changes their PSNR only slightly (SA-LUT 22.54→22.6722.54{\to}22.67 dB, damped 25.09→25.0525.09{\to}25.05 dB), consistent again with the subspace not being the bottleneck, though each projection costs a per-image optimization on top of the teacher. Notably, PREEN lands closer to the expert targets than the projection of its own undamped supervision (22.67→24.6322.67{\to}24.63 dB, Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} 9.70→9.079.70{\to}9.07). The direction of this change (fidelity up, HCorr 0.505→0.4730.505{\to}0.473) matches the training objective’s built-in restraint, since the ℓ2\ell_{2} preset regularizer and identity sampling damp predicted edits. PREEN’s presets are also roughly 4×4\times smaller in norm than the teacher’s projection (median ∥P∥\lVert P\rVert ratio 0.240.24) and only weakly aligned with it in direction (median cosine 0.280.28).

Fourth, the oracle reaches 32.5632.56 dB and HCorr 0.6720.672, far above every method on PSNR, HCorr, and Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} (and best on SSIM, if narrowly), though its LPIPS (0.1370.137) is worse than even the no-edit baseline (0.1270.127). The gap to PREEN on those four metrics is prediction error from observing only (X,Y)(X,Y), which we leave to future work. (The oracle minimizes a CIELAB-weighted reconstruction objective, trading perceptual texture for color/tone fidelity, so it upper-bounds the editor’s color/tone subspace, not its perceptual quality.)

6 Predicted Preset Breakdown

To make the output’s interpretability concrete, Figure S3 shows the actual 2929-parameter presets PREEN predicts for the first five PST50 pairs, namely the 88 global controls and the 2121 per-hue HSL channels, as real editor-slider values in [−1,1][-1,1]. The Vivid column (α=5\alpha\!=\!5) rescales only the 1717 chromaticity parameters, leaving the 1212 tone parameters (the five global tone controls, i.e., contrast, brightness, exposure, highlights, and shadows, plus the seven per-hue luminance channels) unchanged. This is visible as identical tone bars, with the chroma bars (where nonzero) amplified between the two columns.

7 Qualitative Gallery

Failure cases. Figure S4 shows the failure family behind most of PREEN’s worst PST50 cases, namely, target looks that the editor cannot render. We verify this with the per-image oracle fit, the Eq. (1) inversion applied to the ground truth, shown in the third column of the figure. On these samples even the oracle misses the look (oracle Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} 8.78.7–11.011.0 vs. an across-benchmark oracle median of 4.14.1, mean 4.904.90), because the target remaps color (for example, a split-toned near-monochrome or a wholesale palette shift) rather than adjusting existing color. No global preset can express such remapping, regardless of regressor quality. Four of PREEN’s five largest per-image Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} errors fall in this editor-limited family. The last row shows the complementary case, where the oracle matches the target closely (oracle Δ​Ea​b∗\Delta E^{*}_{ab} 4.64.6), whereas PREEN misses it (22.222.2): plain prediction error, i.e., the headroom to the oracle that Section 4.3 of the main paper identifies.

Generalization beyond PST50 (DPST). Figure S5 shows five DPST [8] pairs with distinct content (the main paper showed the first three); there is no paired ground truth, so the comparison is qualitative. PREEN transfers the reference’s color character to unseen content and retains the same α\alpha control.

Extended in-the-wild gallery. Beyond PST50, we apply PREEN to in-the-wild photographs spanning landscape, indoor, and low-light scenes, each paired with a selected reference image. The content images, including those in Figure 1 of the main paper, are the author’s own photographs, and the reference images are free-to-use stock photographs from Pexels (https://www.pexels.com/). Figures S6–S7 show these results. PREEN transfers the global color and tone character of the reference across diverse scenes. As on PST50, looks that hinge on local or otherwise non-global effects are only approximated, since the editor is restricted to global parameters.

8 Backbone Ablation Checkpoints

The exact pretrained checkpoints used in the main paper’s backbone ablation are CLIP ViT-L/14 [10] (openai/clip-vit-large-patch14), DINOv3 ViT-L [12] (facebook/dinov3-vitl16-pretrain-lvd1689m), SigLIP 2 large [13] (google/siglip2-large-patch16-256), and InternViT-300M [2, 3] (OpenGVLab/InternViT-300M-448px). Each backbone runs at its native input resolution, with the MLP head, training schedule, and loss held identical, so rows differ only in the frozen encoder and its native resolution.

9 Additional Implementation Details

The five handcrafted color-statistic features have fixed dimensionality: RGB log-ratio (33), HSL channel-mean difference (33), per-image RGB mean/std for both images (1212), a soft RGB histogram with 1616 bins per channel for both images (9696), and per-channel p10/p50/p90p_{10}/p_{50}/p_{90} percentile differences (99), for 123123 dimensions alongside the two 768768-d CLIP image embeddings. Selected checkpoints occur at 1.11.1k training steps (Phase 1) and 4.64.6k (Phase 2). The Phase 1 inversion optimizes the pre-activation preset with AdamW (learning rate 0.20.2, weight decay 0.010.01) for 1,0001{,}000 steps per pair. AdamW’s default decoupled weight decay (0.010.01) additionally shrinks the pre-activation, separate from the explicit 10−310^{-3} penalty stated in the main paper, both nudging the recovered preset toward neutral. For the single-stage ablation in the main paper, replacing the Phase 2-only variant’s full MLP fine-tuning with a LoRA adapter on a randomly initialized (untrained) MLP base atop the same LoRA-adapted CLIP encoder reaches only Δ​Ea​b∗​ 9.57\Delta E^{*}_{ab}\,9.57 on PST50, versus 9.079.07 for the full pipeline and 9.129.12 for Phase 2-only full fine-tuning, consistent with a low-rank update being underexpressive without the Phase 1 pretrained base.

10 VLM Prompt Template

The main paper reports off-the-shelf foundation-model baselines that predict the 2929-parameter preset directly. Each frontier VLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro [5], Claude Opus 4.8 [1], and Qwen3-VL 235B [9]) receives the identical prompt (Figure S8(b)), with the content and reference images attached (SOURCE and TARGET in the prompt). Each returns a JSON object of 2929 named floats in [−1,1][-1,1], enforced by a structured-output response schema, and we apply the returned preset through the same editor EE used by PREEN. Table S7 compares the two prompt variants of Figure S8. Under the neutral prompt (a), all three models produce substantially larger edits (1.71.7–3.7×3.7\times the guided prompt’s mean per-pixel change |X′−X||X^{\prime}{-}X|) and every metric degrades, while the conservative guidance of (b) recovers the levels reported in the main paper. The guided prompt supplies only generic slider semantics and a magnitude prior (real edits are usually small), with no PST50- or target-specific values, and its two worked examples are a generic neutral-to-warm-vintage preset and a near-zero no-op. Even granted this prior, the VLMs miscalibrate, consistent with editor-grounded calibration being hard to obtain from text prompts alone. VLM outputs are non-deterministic, and we query once per image.

11 User-Study Protocol

The pairwise preference studies of the main paper (Section 4.7) were conducted on Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/). Each study recruited 5050 raters (150150 in total), assigned in balanced groups targeting five independent ratings per image pair. Invalid responses were excluded before analysis. The seven pairings of Figure 6 of the main paper were collected in three studies. Study 1 compared the default against Deep Preset and against Claude. Study 2 compared Vivid against the default, Deep Preset, and Claude. Study 3 compared the default and Vivid against the SA-LUT teacher. Raters saw the reference YY alongside the two candidate edits. The left–right order was randomized per pair, image filenames were anonymized with content hashes, and methods were never named. The two questions, verbatim: “Q1. Which better matches the Style?” (“Color tone, contrast, brightness, overall feel.”) and “Q2. Which looks more beautiful?” (“Independent of Style — which one looks better as a standalone photo?”). Participation was restricted to desktop users. Within a pair’s ratings, majority agreement averages 7474–81%81\% across the three studies and both questions (Fleiss’ κ\kappa 0.150.15–0.340.34), the slight-to-fair agreement range.

Table S8 lists every per-opponent win rate with its confidence interval. The pooled rates of the main paper also count PREEN’s own default as an opponent, a within-system α\alpha comparison rather than a baseline.

12 Full PST50 Results

Figures S9–S12 show every PST50 case: the 5050 paired triples behind every reported number and 5050 unpaired cases (each content image with a further benchmark reference and no expert target) for qualitative coverage only. Each group shows XX, YY, PREEN (α=1\alpha\!=\!1), PREEN Vivid (α=5\alpha\!=\!5), and, for paired cases, the expert target.
